intro: The Winter Palace was the home of the Russian emperors for nearly two centuries. Then, in 1917, revolutionaries stormed it, and a decade later a filmmaker restaged the storming so convincingly that his version replaced history itself.
page_title: Winter Palace: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: The present Winter Palace is the fourth on the site, built from 1754 to 1762 for Empress Elizabeth to the design of her favorite architect, the Italian Bartolomeo Rastrelli, in what became known as the Elizabethan Baroque style. It is an elongated rectangle between the Neva embankment and Palace Square, its principal facade 215 meters long and 30 meters high, green-and-white with white columns, gilded stucco, and a parapet lined with statues and vases. Elizabeth died before it was finished; Catherine the Great and her successors occupied it, and in 1764 Catherine founded the Hermitage Museum that now fills it. The scale is imperial in the literal sense: 1,886 doors, 1,945 windows, 1,500 rooms, 117 staircases, 233,345 square meters of floor. From here the tsars ruled an empire of 22.8 million square kilometers.
sections.heading: Rastrelli's palace

sections.body: In December 1837 a fire gutted the palace. Nicholas I ordered it rebuilt immediately, with the exterior left exactly as Rastrelli had designed it but large parts of the interior redesigned in the tastes of the 1830s. The Jordan Staircase, the state rooms, the Malachite Room: much of what visitors see today is the 19th century's idea of the 18th. Eighty years later the palace became the seat of the Provisional Government, and on the night of 7 November 1917 revolutionary soldiers and sailors entered it and arrested the ministers inside. The actual storming was chaotic and unphotogenic, over quickly, with little of the drama later attached to it.
sections.heading: Fire and revolution

sections.body:
For the tenth anniversary of the Revolution, the Soviet government commissioned Sergei Eisenstein to film it. October (1928) restaged the storming of the Winter Palace with the actual army and navy, close to 11,000 extras, tanks, artillery, and the battleship Aurora. Eisenstein's version was so grand and so visually convincing that stills and clips from the film were printed in Soviet textbooks and documentaries as if they were real historical footage, and the substitution stuck: for generations, the film's storming was the storming. It is the purest case of cinema replacing history.

Three quarters of a century later the palace starred again, this time as itself. Alexander Sokurov's Russian Ark (2002) was shot in a single continuous 96-minute Steadicam take entirely inside the Winter Palace and the Hermitage, following an unnamed narrator through 300 years of Russian history as the rooms themselves become the cast. No film has ever used a building so completely: the palace is not the setting but the subject.

timeline.text: Built to Bartolomeo Rastrelli's design for Empress Elizabeth in the Elizabethan Baroque style.
Catherine the Great founds the Hermitage Museum.
Fire guts the palace; it is rebuilt with the exterior unchanged and new interiors.
Revolutionary forces storm the Winter Palace and arrest the Provisional Government.
Eisenstein's October premieres, its restaged storming replacing the real one in public memory.
Sokurov's Russian Ark is filmed in a single 96-minute take inside the palace.
